note: Summarises evaluation metrics plus the toolkits and datasets available to run them, a practical starting kit.
title: Fairness in Large Language Models: A Taxonomic Survey
explain_beginner: This survey asks a basic question, once a language model is expected to be fair, what does fairness even mean for a system like this, and how is that different from fairness in older, simpler machine learning models. The authors point out that fairness research built for things like loan approval algorithms does not transfer cleanly to a model that generates open ended text, because there is no single protected outcome to check, like approve or deny, there is an entire generated sentence that can be subtly biased in tone, association, or omission. The paper works through why large language models pick up bias in the first place, tracing it to training data and design choices, then surveys how researchers try to measure fairness and the tools built to promote it. It found that the field has produced many metrics and toolkits but no unified standard, and that fairness concepts genuinely need new definitions for generative systems rather than borrowed ones. It does not settle which definition should become the standard, and it explicitly leaves that question open for future work rather than answering it.
explain_business: The direct business relevance is as a reference document when scoping a fairness audit for a language model product, not as a ready made compliance tool. Because the paper catalogs existing toolkits and datasets for bias evaluation, a team building an internal review process can use it to avoid reinventing evaluation infrastructure that already exists in the open research community. The risk it implicitly flags is that fairness metrics built for older classification systems, the kind many compliance teams already know, do not directly apply to generative text systems, so a company relying on legacy fairness testing frameworks may be checking the wrong thing entirely for a chatbot or writing assistant. There is no dollar figure or deployment timeline attached to this paper, it is foundational rather than applied. It becomes operationally useful the moment an organization needs to build or select a bias testing toolkit for a language model product, since the survey's compiled resource list shortens that search, though someone still has to validate that a chosen toolkit actually works for the specific language and use case being deployed.
explain_practitioner: Published in ACM SIGKDD Explorations Newsletter, this is a categorical survey rather than an experimental paper. It begins with the factors that introduce bias into large language models, moves through how fairness is conceptualized specifically for these systems as distinct from classical machine learning fairness, and then summarizes both the metrics used to evaluate bias and the algorithms proposed to promote fairness. It also compiles toolkits and datasets built for bias evaluation, functioning as a resource index for anyone building an evaluation pipeline. A related tutorial version of this work, presented at a major data mining conference as a three hour session, signals that the field treated this taxonomy as a teaching reference rather than a one off publication. The authors close by naming open research challenges and unanswered questions directly, without resolving them, which is the honest limitation of any survey of this kind, it maps the literature accurately but cannot tell a practitioner which specific metric or toolkit will generalize to a new model or a new language, since most of the underlying studies were built and tested on English language models.
